J1_line_asserts_challenged_proposition.justification: The response challenges "A locale isomorphism is defined merely as a continuous map f such that f = h^{op} for some frame homomorphism h, without requiring h to be an isomorphism." First-choice line 17, ":$f = h^{\text{op}}$ for some [[Definition:Frame Homomorphism|frame homomorphism]]", is the right-hand side of the biconditional begun at lines 14-16 ("By definition of locale isomorphism: f is a locale isomorphism {{iff}}:"), so with its introducing lines it asserts exactly that characterization. The contrast with line 7, whose condition is "$f = h^{\text{op}}$ for some isomorphism $h$ in $\mathbf{Frm}$", shows the qualifier is missing here and not merely implicit elsewhere. Active assumptions: P3, P4 (f : S_1 -> S_2 a continuous map of Loc) and line 2 (Loc is the dual of Frm).

J2_evidence_specified.justification: The response names a concrete instance and the two facts that make it bite: "The constant map from the locale of the real line to the one-point locale gives a frame homomorphism h:{0,1} -> O(R) that is not an isomorphism, yet according to line 0017 the map would be called a locale isomorphism, though it is not an isomorphism in Loc." Its reasoning fixes h explicitly ("sending 0 to empty set, 1 to whole line") and states why it is not an isomorphism ("not surjective"). Both locales, the frame homomorphism and the failure mode are given.

J3_evidence_check.justification: Model-assisted judgment: I followed the supplied argument step by step and found no gap; no computation was possible or needed, so no script or Lean file. The steps, each checked against the source's own active assumptions: (i) O(R) (the topology of the real line) is a frame and the two-element chain {0,1} is the frame of the one-point locale; (ii) the map h : {0,1} -> O(R) with 0 |-> empty set and 1 |-> R preserves finite meets (including the top) and arbitrary joins (including the empty join), so it is a frame homomorphism -- this is the response's h; (iii) by line 2 (Loc is the dual of Frm), morphisms L1 -> L2 of Loc are exactly frame homomorphisms O(L2) -> O(L1), so f = h^{op} is a continuous map of Loc as P4 requires, and it therefore satisfies line 17's stated condition; (iv) h is not an isomorphism in Frm because it is not surjective -- (0,1) is an open set of R distinct from the empty set and from R -- so by lines 4-7 (Isomorphism iff Isomorphism in Dual Category) f is not an isomorphism of Loc. Hence line 17's condition holds for an f that is not an isomorphism of Loc, while the theorem P6 that this proof is establishing says a locale isomorphism is exactly an isomorphism of Loc. So the condition at line 17 cannot be equivalent to being a locale isomorphism: the line is false as written, and the witness refutes it on the source's own terms rather than a weakened version. (As the response also observes, the condition as written is satisfied by every continuous map of Loc, so it is vacuous.)

J4_consequence_overreach.justification: The response's stated consequence stays with the line: "So line 0017 is false: it defines locale isomorphism merely as any frame homomorphism (not necessarily iso)", and it deliberately clears the neighbouring lines instead of sweeping them in -- "line 0006 ... That is true by dual category property", "line 0010-0012 ... That's true definition". It never asserts that the theorem P6 itself is false, which would have been the overreach available here. Correctly scoped.

notes: For a second reader: the packet does not quote [[Definition:Locale Isomorphism]], so the falsity of line 17 cannot be checked directly against that definition. What makes the witness decisive without it is internal: the proof's goal P6 equates 'locale isomorphism' with 'isomorphism of Loc', and the witness exhibits a continuous map satisfying line 17's condition that is not an isomorphism of Loc (its frame homomorphism is not surjective). Whatever the linked definition says, line 17's condition cannot be it unless P6 fails. The standard facts I relied on and the response left implicit are: morphism direction in Loc = Frm^{op} (given by the source at line 2), that bottom |-> bottom, top |-> top from the two-element frame is a frame homomorphism, and that O(R) has elements other than the empty set and R. A reader who treats a dropped word in a cited definition as a typographical rather than a mathematical defect might grade J1 differently; I took the line as written, as the task framing directs.
